commands.short: The komando skill and guard in your AI agents: install, uninstall
commands.example:
komando agent skill install --dry-run
  komando agent skill install
  komando agent skill uninstall --dry-run
  komando agent skill uninstall

commands.short: Add the komando skill to Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI
commands.long:
Teaches Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and Gemini CLI to use komando safely.
Then restart the agent. In Codex, also approve the guard once in /hooks.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first.

It adds the komando skill (komando/SKILL.md) to the folders AI agents read
skills from: ~/.claude/skills (Claude Code) and ~/.agents/skills (Codex,
Cursor, Gemini CLI and others). The agent then uses komando by itself
whenever a task touches a server, database, cache or storage.

It also adds a guard: before the agent reads a file or runs a shell command
on this computer, komando checks it and stops the ones that would read
secrets (~/.komando, private keys, .env files, credential stores, all
environment variables at once) or use ssh around komando. It goes into
Claude Code (.claude/settings.json), and into Cursor (.cursor/hooks.json),
Gemini CLI (.gemini/settings.json, v0.26+) and Codex (.codex/hooks.json;
approve it once in /hooks) where their folders exist. Skip it with
--no-guard.

Safe to run again, for example after an update: a changed file is kept as
.bak. `komando agent skill uninstall` takes the skill and the guard out
again.
commands.example:
komando agent skill install             # for every project on this computer
  komando agent skill install --project   # only for the folder you are in
  komando agent skill install --dry-run   # show where it would go

flags.name: no-guard
flags.usage: do not add the guard that keeps AI agents away from secret files on this computer

flags.name: project
flags.usage: use the current folder instead of your home folder

commands.short: Take the komando skill and guard out of your AI agents
commands.long:
Removes what `komando agent skill install` added: komando/SKILL.md in
~/.claude/skills and ~/.agents/skills, and komando's guard entries in
.claude/settings.json, .cursor/hooks.json, .gemini/settings.json and
.codex/hooks.json. Everything else in those files stays; a changed file is
kept as .bak. Taking the guard away from an AI agent lets it read secret
files on this computer again, so an agent needs a person's yes (--yes).

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first; when it removes komando's
guard from an AI agent's settings: it weakens a safety check: a person's yes
(--yes).
commands.example:
komando agent skill uninstall             # from your home folder
  komando agent skill uninstall --project   # from the folder you are in
  komando agent skill uninstall --dry-run   # show what it would remove

flags.name: project
flags.usage: use the current folder instead of your home folder

confirm.when: when it removes komando's guard from an AI agent's settings

commands.short: Check that no audit record was changed, added or removed outside komando
commands.example:
komando audit check
  komando audit check -o json

commands.short: Show the audit log: who did what, where, and the result
commands.long:
Every change komando makes, and every blocked attempt, is a sealed record in
~/.komando/store.db: when, who (and which AI agent), the command, its
targets and whether it worked. The newest entries come last.

--since and --until take how long ago (30m, 12h, 7d), today, yesterday,
or a time (2026-11-07, '2026-11-07 14:30', 2026-11-07T14:30:00Z); a time
without a zone is this computer's. --since keeps entries from that moment
on, --until those before it. With either, every match is shown unless -n
is given.
commands.example:
komando audit list                      # the last 50
  komando audit list -n 0 --target @prod  # everything about @prod
  komando audit list --command host. --failed
  komando audit list --since 2h           # everything in the last two hours
  komando audit list --since yesterday --until today --target @prod
  komando audit list --actor claude --since 7d   # what Claude Code did this week

flags.usage: only commands that start with this (like exec, fs.)

flags.usage: only actions that failed or were blocked

flags.usage: the newest N entries (0 = all; with --since or --until, all unless given)

flags.name: since
flags.usage: only entries from this time on: 2h, 7d, today, 2026-11-07 or '2026-11-07 14:30'

flags.name: target
flags.usage: only entries for these servers or conns (a selector, like @prod)

flags.name: until
flags.usage: only entries before this time (the same forms as --since)

commands.short: Caches (Redis, Valkey, memcached): read and change keys
commands.long:
Read and change keys in Redis, Valkey or memcached. Add a cache with
`komando cache redis add`.

get, keys and info only read. set changes data (a protected cache asks
first); rm deletes keys, so it also needs --allow-dangerous. `cache redis
raw` sends any command, but only reads unless --write; commands that flush,
block, run scripts or reconfigure the server also need --allow-dangerous.
commands.example:
komando cache redis add prod-redis redis://default@10.0.0.7:6379/0 --via web1 --ask-password
  komando cache info prod-redis
  komando cache keys prod-redis 'session:*'
  komando cache get prod-redis session:42
  komando cache set prod-redis maintenance on --ttl 30m --dry-run

  komando cache get prod-redis leaderboard --limit 10

commands.long:

limit, eviction policy, clients, keys per database and the hit rate. A
SECTION (server, clients, memory, persistence, stats, replication, cpu,
commandstats, keyspace, ...) or --all shows the raw INFO fields.
commands.example:
komando cache info prod-redis
  komando cache info prod-redis memory
  komando cache info prod-redis --all

commands.short: TLS certificates: when do they expire, and do they verify
commands.example:
komando cert check web1                           # certificates on the server
  komando cert check @web --warn 30d
  komando cert check https://shop.example.com --warn 14d

commands.short: Check when the certificates of servers and websites expire
commands.long:
Reads certificates and says when they expire. It only reads.

A server (or @group, tag:, ...): komando looks for the certificates the
server uses: certbot's /etc/letsencrypt/live/*/cert.pem and the files that
nginx (ssl_certificate), haproxy (crt) and apache (SSLCertificateFile) name,
plus any --path. Files that need root are read with sudo only when sudo
works without a password; komando never asks for one. Only the CERTIFICATE
blocks of a file leave the server: a private key in the same file never
does. When certbot is there, the state of its renewal timer is shown too.

A website (https://example.com, example.com:443) or a conn that uses TLS:
komando connects from this computer (or through --via, or the conn's own
--via), reads the certificate the server sends and checks that it is
trusted and matches the name.

A certificate that expires within --warn (default 30d), has expired, is not
trusted, or a certbot renewal that failed is a problem: the command then
exits 1 (code CERT_PROBLEMS), like `komando doctor`.
commands.example:
komando cert check web1
  komando cert check @prod --warn 14d
  komando cert check https://shop.example.com api.example.com:8443
  komando cert check https://intranet.local --via bastion
  komando cert check web1 --path /etc/ssl/private/site.pem

flags.name: path
flags.usage: also check this certificate file (or folder) on the servers

flags.name: via
flags.usage: reach websites through this server or VPN (a --via path)

flags.name: warn
flags.usage: flag certificates that expire within this time (like 30d, 72h)

commands.short: Kubernetes clusters: save, check, read logs, roll out, scale
commands.long:
TARGET is a Kubernetes cluster saved with `komando cluster kubernetes add`
or a Swarm manager server. Reads need nothing; restart, scale and apply
change the cluster (protected targets need --yes; try --dry-run); rm needs
--allow-dangerous. Anything else: `cluster kubernetes raw` passes the native
kubectl command, read-only unless --write.

A cluster's usual namespace is its kubeconfig context's; change it with
`komando cluster kubernetes edit NAME --option namespace=shop`, or name one
per command with --namespace.
commands.example:
komando cluster kubernetes add prod-k8s k8s://api.cluster.example:6443 --credential prod-kubeconfig
  komando cluster status prod-k8s                     # version, nodes, what is not healthy
  komando cluster list prod-k8s pods --namespace shop
  komando cluster logs prod-k8s deploy/api --namespace shop -f
  komando cluster deploy prod-k8s deploy/api --image ghcr.io/acme/api:1.4.3 --namespace shop --wait

commands.short: Apply Kubernetes YAML or deploy a Swarm stack
commands.long:
Kubernetes: applies every object in FILE server-side and says per object
whether it was created, configured or unchanged. --dry-run asks the server
what would change and shows it as a diff (Secret values stay hidden; a
changed value shows as "[hidden, changed]"). Objects without a namespace go
to --namespace; one that names another namespace is refused.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first; on a protected server or
conn, a person's yes (--yes) as well.

A field another field manager owns (an autoscaler's replicas, a kubectl
edit) stops the apply with K8S_CONFLICT naming that manager, and nothing
is applied. --force-conflicts takes those fields over, as
`kubectl apply --server-side --force-conflicts` does.

Swarm: deploys FILE (a compose file) as the stack --stack; --dry-run checks
the file with `docker stack config` on the manager.
commands.example:
komando cluster apply prod-k8s --file app.yaml --dry-run
  komando cluster apply prod-k8s --file app.yaml
  komando cluster apply swarm1 --file compose.yml --stack shop

flags.name: file
flags.usage: YAML file ('-' for stdin)

flags.name: force-conflicts
flags.usage: Kubernetes: take over fields another field manager owns

flags.name: namespace
flags.usage: Kubernetes namespace (default: the context's, else default)

flags.name: stack
flags.usage: Swarm: the stack name

commands.usage: komando cluster deploy TARGET TYPE/NAME --image IMAGE [flags]
commands.short: Roll out a new image
commands.long:
Sets the image of a deployment, statefulset or daemonset (Kubernetes) or a
service (Swarm). With several containers, name one with --container (or
write --image NAME=IMAGE). --wait stays until every replica runs the new
image, the rollout fails, or --timeout (default 5m) passes; go back with
`komando cluster rollback`.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first; on a protected server or
conn, a person's yes (--yes) as well.
commands.example:
komando cluster deploy prod-k8s deployment/api --image ghcr.io/acme/api:1.4.3 --namespace shop --wait
  komando cluster deploy prod-k8s deployment/api --image ghcr.io/acme/api:1.4.3 --namespace shop --wait --dry-run
  komando cluster deploy swarm1 service/web --image nginx:1.27 --wait

flags.name: container
flags.usage: which container gets the image (needed when there are several)

flags.name: image
flags.usage: the new image, like ghcr.io/acme/api:1.4.3 (or CONTAINER=IMAGE)

flags.name: namespace
flags.usage: Kubernetes namespace (default: the context's, else default)

flags.name: wait
flags.usage: wait until the rollout finishes (or fails; --timeout, default 5m)

commands.short: Ask for an authenticator app code in the approval window (person only)
commands.long:
Sets up a one-time code (TOTP, like a bank or GitHub login) for komando's
"Allow once" window: once on, allowing an AI agent's --yes,
--allow-dangerous or --reveal needs the 6-digit code from the authenticator
app on your phone, not just a click. On macOS the window asks for Touch ID,
an Apple Watch or your login password instead and does not use the code; it
stays set for Linux, BSD and Windows on the same vault. Only a person at a
terminal can turn it on (the secret is shown once, here); turning it off
needs --yes, so that code too.

Safety: only a person at a terminal can run it.

commands.short: Print one setting
commands.example:
komando config get parallel
  komando config get host_key_policy -o text

commands.short: Change a setting
commands.long:
Settings:
  host_key_policy  accept-new | strict | off
      how server identity is checked: accept-new pins a new server's key, strict needs `host ssh trust` first, off checks nothing (needs --yes)
  default_user     a login name
      user for servers that have none (empty: your own user name)
  default_timeout  duration > 0
      how long a remote command may run (--timeout overrides it)
  connect_timeout  duration > 0
      how long connecting may take (--connect-timeout overrides it)
  parallel         1 or more
      how many servers a command works on at once (-P overrides it)
  max_output_bytes 1024 or more
      output kept per stream and server, in bytes (--max-output overrides it)
  audit            on | off
      keep the audit log (turning it off needs --yes)
  audit_sql        full | hash | off
      how SQL text is kept in the audit log: hash keeps a SHA-256 so repeated queries can be matched (off needs --yes)
  audit_syslog     udp://HOST:514 | tcp://HOST:514 | tls://HOST:6514 | off
      also send each audit record to a log server (syslog, RFC 5424); changing it needs --yes
  mask_personal    protected | all | off
      where AI agents see email addresses, phone numbers, card numbers and IBANs hidden: on protected servers and conns (the default), on all, or nowhere (less needs --yes)
  login_for        duration
      how long `komando login SERVER` keeps a server's login for later commands (an AI agent's too)
  approval_languageauto | en | id
      the language of the approval window: auto follows the system language (Indonesian when it is id, else English)
  vpn_idle         duration, 0 = never
      a VPN kept up with `vpn KIND start` is closed after this long unused

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first; when the setting turns a
check off: it weakens a safety check: a person's yes (--yes).

To go back to a default, set the value from the DEFAULT column of `komando
config show`.
commands.example:
komando config set parallel 20 --dry-run
  komando config set parallel 20
  komando config set default_timeout 10m
  komando config set audit_sql hash

confirm.when: when the setting turns a check off

commands.short: Keep the vault key in the OS keychain instead of store.key
commands.long:
Moves the vault's key out of the store.key file into the operating system's
keychain, so a copy of ~/.komando (a backup, a synced folder) no longer
opens the vault or its secrets. The vault gets a new key as it moves, so a
copy of store.key made before opens nothing either, and the vault keeps
every secret. --off moves the key back into store.key, which needs --yes.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first; when it turns the keychain
off: it weakens a safety check: a person's yes (--yes); without --off: only
a person at a terminal can run it.

Only a person at a terminal moves the key in: the keychain may ask them to
unlock it, and an AI agent or a script cannot answer that.
commands.example:
komando config vault keychain --dry-run
  komando config vault keychain
  komando config vault keychain --off --dry-run
  komando config vault keychain --off --yes   # after a person's yes

flags.name: off
flags.usage: move the key back into store.key (needs --yes)

confirm.when: when it turns the keychain off

commands.short: Change the vault passphrase and encrypt the secrets again (person only)
commands.long:
Re-encrypts every secret in the vault under a new passphrase, so you can
change KOMANDO_VAULT_PASS without losing your secrets. A vault whose key is
in store.key or in the OS keychain gets a passphrase this way, and the old
key is removed once the new vault is saved and read back.

Safety: only a person at a terminal can run it.

The vault is opened the usual way: with KOMANDO_VAULT_PASS, store.key or the
keychain. When KOMANDO_VAULT_PASS does not open a passphrase vault (you
changed it already, say), komando asks for the current passphrase. Then it
asks for the new one twice, hidden; it needs 15 or more characters. Every
secret is decrypted before anything is written: if one cannot be, nothing
changes.

Afterwards, put the new passphrase in KOMANDO_VAULT_PASS wherever you set it
(your shell profile, a password manager, a launch agent), and restart any
background tunnel or VPN session komando runs: they still hold the old key.

--off goes back to a new random key in store.key (needs --yes): a copy of
~/.komando then opens the vault again. `komando config vault keychain` can
move that key into the OS keychain.

Only a person at a terminal can run it: an AI agent that chose the
passphrase, or put the key back in store.key, could open the vault on its
own. Anyone can preview it with --dry-run.
commands.example:
komando config vault passphrase --dry-run
  komando config vault passphrase   # asks for the new passphrase twice, hidden
  komando config vault passphrase --off --dry-run
  komando config vault passphrase --off --yes   # after a person's yes

flags.name: off
flags.usage: back to a random key in store.key (needs --yes)

commands.short: Conns (databases, caches, queues, ...): add, change, remove
commands.long:
A conn is a database, cache, message queue, file storage, cluster or
registry komando talks to directly. The kind comes from the URL scheme
(`komando conn kinds` lists them). Passwords never go in the URL: store them
with `komando credential password add` and pass --password-ref. Use --via
HOST when the conn is only reachable from a server.

Conns share names and selectors (@group, tag:x, glob, all) with servers.
commands.example:
komando conn add prod-db postgres://app@10.0.0.9/shop --password-ref credential:prod-db-pass
  komando test prod-db                              # does it answer and let komando in?
  komando conn edit prod-db --via web1 --dry-run
  komando conn rm prod-db                           # from komando only

commands.short: Add a conn (the URL scheme sets its kind)
commands.long:
Add a conn (the URL scheme sets its kind).

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first.
commands.example:
komando conn add prod-db postgres://app@10.0.0.5:5432/app --via web1 --password-ref credential:prod-db-pass --protected
  komando conn add prod-db postgres://app@10.0.0.5:5432/app --via web1 --password-ref credential:prod-db-pass --protected --dry-run
  komando conn add shop mysql://shop@db.internal/shop --group shop
  komando conn add local sqlite:///var/lib/app.db
  komando conn add cache redis://default@10.0.0.7:6379/0 --via web1 --password-ref credential:redis-pass
  komando conn add backups 's3://AKIAEXAMPLE@my-bucket/db?region=eu-west-1' --password-ref credential:s3-secret
  komando conn add prod-db postgres://app@10.0.0.5/app --via web1 --ask-password   # type it now (hidden)
  komando conn add prod-db postgres://app@10.0.0.5/app --via web1 --login ask      # type it at every connect; never stored

  komando credential certificate list

commands.short: Trust a CA for the servers its patterns match (person only)
commands.long:
Trusts the CA in --key (a .pub file) for the host names in --hosts, or reads
the @cert-authority lines of a known_hosts file (--from); its @revoked lines
go on the never-trust list. A pattern names at least the domain
(*.corp.example, web*.corp.example, 10.1.2.*): '*' and '*.com' are refused.
--dry-run shows the patterns as they are kept and the servers they match
now. Only a person at a terminal can add a CA: it trusts every server it
ever signs.

Safety: only a person at a terminal can run it.
commands.example:
komando credential certificate add corp --key ~/corp-ca.pub --hosts '*.corp.example' --dry-run
  komando credential certificate add corp --from ~/.ssh/known_hosts --dry-run

flags.name: from
flags.usage: a known_hosts file: read its @cert-authority and @revoked lines

flags.name: hosts
flags.usage: server name patterns the CA may vouch for (*.corp.example,10.1.2.*)

flags.name: key
flags.usage: the CA's public key file (.pub)

  komando credential certificate remove corp

commands.usage: komando credential key add NAME FILE [flags]
commands.short: Add a private key file you already have (komando keeps its path)
commands.long:
Adds a private key file you already have to komando's key list; the file
stays where it is. For a key with a passphrase, save the passphrase as a
password credential and pass --passphrase-credential NAME.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first.

An OpenSSH user certificate next to the key (FILE-cert.pub) is used at
login, as ssh does; --cert names one kept somewhere else.
commands.example:
komando credential key add personal ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 --dry-run
  komando credential key add personal ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
  komando credential key add corp ~/.ssh/id_corp --cert ~/.ssh/corp-ca/id_corp-cert.pub
  komando credential key add work ~/.ssh/id_work --passphrase-credential id-pass

flags.name: cert
flags.usage: an OpenSSH user certificate for the key (default: FILE-cert.pub next to it, if there)

flags.name: passphrase-credential
flags.usage: the password credential that opens an encrypted key file

commands.short: Make a new SSH key pair (ed25519 by default)
commands.long:
Makes a key pair like ssh-keygen and adds it to komando's key list. The
private key is kept in komando's sealed store, never in a file: komando
hands it to ssh-agent when another program needs it (host ssh-command). Put
the public part on servers with `komando credential key install`. RSA keys
need at least 3072 bits.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first.
commands.example:
komando credential key create deploy --dry-run
  komando credential key create deploy
  komando credential key create legacy --type rsa -b 4096 -C ops@example.com

flags.name: bits
flags.usage: key size: RSA 3072-16384 (default 4096), ECDSA 256|384|521

flags.name: comment
flags.usage: public key comment (default komando-NAME)

flags.name: type
flags.usage: ed25519 | rsa | ecdsa

commands.short: Change a key's passphrase credential or certificate
commands.long:
Sets where komando finds the passphrase of an encrypted key. Store the
passphrase with `komando credential password add NAME` first and pass
--passphrase-credential NAME; --unset passphrase-credential clears it.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first.

--cert FILE gives the key an OpenSSH user certificate (for a key komando
made, or one kept away from the key file); --unset cert goes back to
FILE-cert.pub next to the key.
commands.example:
komando credential key edit work --passphrase-credential work-key-pass --dry-run
  komando credential key edit work --passphrase-credential work-key-pass
  komando credential key edit work --unset passphrase-credential
  komando credential key edit deploy --cert ~/Downloads/deploy-cert.pub

flags.name: cert
flags.usage: an OpenSSH user certificate for the key

flags.name: passphrase-credential
flags.usage: the password credential that opens an encrypted key file

flags.usage: clear this setting: passphrase-credential, cert

commands.short: Install a public key in ~/.ssh/authorized_keys (like ssh-copy-id)
commands.long:
Installs a public key on servers, like ssh-copy-id. NAME is a key in
komando's key list or a .pub file. komando logs in the way each server is
set up now (a password, for example) and appends the key to
~/.ssh/authorized_keys unless it is already there. With --set-default the
servers then log in with this key.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first; with --public-key-file: only
a person at a terminal can run it; on a protected server or conn, a person's
yes (--yes) as well.

With --public-key-file and --user (no NAME), a person installs a phone's key
for that user on one server, always behind the server's own komando gate
(restrict, ssh-gate --here; from= with --from-address).
commands.example:
komando credential key install deploy @web --dry-run
  komando credential key install deploy @web --set-default
  komando credential key install ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub web1
  komando credential key install web1 --user anna --public-key-file anna-phone.pub --from-address 10.0.0.0/8

flags.name: from-address
flags.usage: the addresses the device logs in from, as the server sees them

flags.name: public-key-file
flags.usage: a device's public key file (a phone's): install it for --user behind the server's own komando gate

flags.name: set-default
flags.usage: servers that got the key log in with it from now on

flags.name: user
flags.usage: the user the device logs in as (never root)

flags.name: limit
flags.usage: show at most this many (0 = all)

commands.short: Remove a key (from komando only)
commands.long:
Removes the key from komando's key list. --delete-file also deletes the
private key komando keeps for a key it made (credential key create), for
good; a key file you added stays on disk.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first; with --delete-file:
dangerous, it cannot be undone: a person types the name to go on, and an AI
agent or a script needs --allow-dangerous.
commands.example:
komando credential key remove old-ci --dry-run
  komando credential key remove old-ci
  komando credential key remove deploy --delete-file --dry-run

flags.name: delete-file
flags.usage: also delete the private key komando keeps (only keys komando made)

commands.usage: komando credential key rename NAME NEW [flags]
commands.short: Rename a key, and every server that uses it
commands.long:
Gives a key in komando's key list a new name; the servers that use it
follow. A key komando made (credential key create) lives in the sealed
store, so no file moves; a key added from elsewhere (credential key add)
stays where it is. Public keys already installed on servers keep their
comment: they still work, since the key itself does not change.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first.
commands.example:
komando credential key rename old-ci ci --dry-run
  komando credential key rename deploy deploy-2026

commands.short: Show a key's public part, or a person its private key
commands.long:
Shows a key's type, fingerprint and public part. A person at a terminal can
add --reveal to print the private key of a key komando made (it is kept in
komando's sealed store, with no file), for example to keep a copy in a
password manager; from a program without a terminal (the Komando Mac app),
komando first asks the person in its own window. A key added with
`credential key add` is a file you have already: --reveal names its path. AI
agents never get a private key.
commands.example:
komando credential key show deploy
  komando credential key show deploy --dry-run
  komando credential key show deploy --reveal --dry-run   # after a person's yes
  komando credential key show deploy --reveal > deploy.key   # after a person's yes

commands.usage: komando credential key uninstall NAME TARGET [flags]
commands.short: Take a public key off servers' authorized_keys
commands.long:
NAME is a key in komando's key list, a .pub file, or a public key line.
Every line with that key is removed from ~/.ssh/authorized_keys of the login
user, or of --user NAME (with sudo), or of every user on the server with
--all-users (with sudo: someone who left may have put the key in another
account too; the dry run names each user whose file holds it). The file
keeps its owner and mode, and is read and written as its user. Revoking the
key komando itself logs in with needs --allow-dangerous: you would lock
yourself out. --dry-run counts the lines it would remove.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first; when it is the key komando
logs in with: dangerous, it cannot be undone: a person types the name to go
on, and an AI agent or a script needs --allow-dangerous; on a protected
server or conn, a person's yes (--yes) as well.
commands.example:
komando credential key uninstall ~/keys/alice.pub @web --dry-run
  komando credential key uninstall old-deploy @web --user deploy --dry-run
  komando credential key uninstall ~/keys/alice.pub @web --all-users --dry-run

flags.usage: edit every user's authorized_keys on the server (uses sudo)

flags.name: user
flags.usage: edit this user's authorized_keys instead of the login user's (uses sudo)

commands.short: Save a password, typed hidden or from a variable or a pipe
commands.long:
Saves or replaces a password or a token. Replacing one that a production
server or database uses asks first: it changes how komando logs in there.
With --new it only saves a new one: when NAME is in the vault already it
stops with SECRET_EXISTS and leaves the stored value alone.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first.

A value from a pipe loses the line breaks at its end (echo and pbpaste add
one). Spaces are kept, since a password can hold them; komando warns when
the value starts or ends with one, so a stray space copied with a password
is noticed. At the terminal, paste or type the value after the prompt
appears.
commands.example:
komando credential password add web1-pass --dry-run
  komando credential password add web1-pass   # type or paste it after the prompt, nothing is shown
  komando credential password add db-pass --new --from-env VALUE

flags.usage: read the value from this environment variable

flags.name: new
flags.usage: only save one that is not saved yet; a taken NAME stops with SECRET_EXISTS

commands.usage: komando credential password rename NAME NEW [flags]
commands.short: Rename a password and every reference to it (value never shown)
commands.long:
Rename a password and every reference to it (value never shown).

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first.
commands.example:
komando credential password rename db-pass db-pass-old --dry-run
  komando credential password rename db-pass db-pass-old

flags.usage: replace NEW when it exists (what uses NEW then gets the value of NAME)

commands.short: Show that a password is saved and what uses it, its value hidden
commands.long:
Says whether the secret exists and what uses it, without its value. A person
at a terminal can add --reveal to print it; from a program without a
terminal (the Komando Mac app), komando first asks the person in its own
window. AI agents never get the value (they reference it as credential:NAME
instead). A warning says when the value starts or ends with a space, tab or
line break, a common cause of a failing login; 'komando secret check NAME'
lets a person compare it.
commands.example:
komando credential password show db-pass
  komando credential password show db-pass --dry-run
  komando credential password show db-pass --reveal --dry-run   # after a person's yes
  komando credential password show db-pass --reveal | pbcopy   # after a person's yes

commands.short: Run a command here with saved credentials in its environment
commands.long:
Starts COMMAND on this computer with the --env values in its environment. A
value credential:NAME is read from the vault right before the program
starts, so it is never in the command line or the shell history. The program
starts directly, without a shell, with your environment minus komando's own
KOMANDO_* variables and the values that unlock the vault. For an AI agent
with secrets, --env may add variables but never replace one komando sets
(HOME, PATH, USER, LANG, ...), and may not set what decides which code or
settings the program loads: LD_PRELOAD, DYLD_*, NODE_OPTIONS, PYTHON*,
BASH_ENV, a pager, an editor, an askpass helper, an rc file, a proxy, GIT_*,
SSH_*, XDG_*, a tool's config file (KUBECONFIG, DOCKER_CONFIG,
*_CONFIG_FILE, AWS_*_FILE, NPM_CONFIG_*) or a toolchain's (CC, CXX, GOFLAGS,
GOTOOLCHAIN, CARGO_*, RUSTC_WRAPPER, JAVA_HOME, MAVEN_OPTS). The program
gets HOME, USER and LOGNAME from your OS account (USERPROFILE on Windows),
LANG, LC_*, TERM, TMPDIR, TZ, the Windows system folders, a system PATH and
its --env values.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first; when an AI agent hands a
saved secret to a program: it weakens a safety check: a person's yes
(--yes).

The program's output goes through komando's masking: a vault value it prints
shows as [credential:NAME]. komando exits with the program's exit code.

For an AI agent every credential:NAME needs a person's yes (--yes, then
komando's window names the secrets and the program), since the program
could print a value in a form masking does not know. A secret a protected
server, conn or VPN uses asks a person at a terminal too.
commands.example:
komando credential run --dry-run --env TOKEN=credential:gh-token -- ./deploy.sh
  komando credential run --env PGPASSWORD=credential:db-main -- psql -h 10.0.0.5 -U app
  komando credential run -e AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=credential:aws-ci -e AWS_REGION=eu-west-1 -- terraform plan

flags.usage: put KEY=VALUE or KEY=credential:NAME in the program's environment (repeatable)

commands.short: Run a query on a BigQuery database (read only by default)
commands.long:
Run a query on a BigQuery database (read only by default).

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first; when the query deletes data
(DROP, DELETE without WHERE, KILL, ...): dangerous, it cannot be undone: a
person types the name to go on, and an AI agent or a script needs
--allow-dangerous.

More about query:
A run stops after 30s unless --timeout (or the statement_timeout option in
the database URL) allows more. Placeholders take their values from
--arg, in order. -o csv and -o tsv print every row (up to --limit, if
given) for spreadsheets and scripts.
SQL that starts with a -- comment: pass it after -- or with -f -.

SQL Server has no read-only transaction: without --write komando rolls the
SQL back, and a statement it does not know as a read (a bare procedure
name, EXEC) needs --write. Its placeholders are @p1, @p2, ...

Oracle: placeholders are :1, :2, ... A PL/SQL block (BEGIN ... END;) runs
to the end of the text or to a line with only /, and needs --write and
--allow-dangerous. DDL (CREATE, ALTER, DROP, GRANT) commits on its own in
Oracle, so it needs --write, goes on its own, and a dry run only reports it.

ClickHouse has no transactions: without --write every request carries the
server's own readonly=1, and a statement that is not a read (INSERT, ALTER,
CREATE, ...) needs --write, goes on its own, and a dry run only reports it.
Placeholders are {p1:String}, {p2:UInt64}, ... (named p1, p2, with a type).

Snowflake has no read-only mode komando can switch on, and each statement
is a session of its own: without --write komando sends only what it rates
as a read, and a statement that is not a read needs --write, goes on its
own, and a dry run only reports it. Log in with a role that may only
read. Placeholders are ?.

BigQuery: each statement first goes as a dry run, which runs nothing and
says what BigQuery sees and how many bytes it would read (which is what
BigQuery bills). Without --write only a SELECT runs. A query that would
read more than --max-bytes (default 10GB) does not run, and the job
carries that cap too. A write needs --write, goes on its own, and
--write --dry-run shows BigQuery's dry run. Placeholders are ?; the values
go as STRING, so write CAST(? AS INT64) for a number.

On MongoDB the text is a command document in JSON, its first key
naming it ({"find": ...}, {"aggregate": ...}, {"update": ...}). komando rates
it as it rates SQL: what it does not know as a read needs --write. "$db"
picks another database than the URL's.
commands.example:
komando database bigquery query bq "select count(*) from shop.orders"
  komando database bigquery query bq --write --dry-run "update shop.orders set status = 'paid' where id = 42"
  komando database bigquery query bq "select count(*) from shop.orders" --max-bytes 50GB

Open komando's SQL shell on a BigQuery database.

only /) and runs with the checks of query: read-only unless the shell was
started with --write, destructive statements only with --allow-dangerous,
and every statement is audited. A statement runs in its own transaction.

table, \l databases, \dn schemas, \du roles, \x switches expanded rows,
\timing shows how long each statement took, \i FILE runs a file, and a
statement ending in \G is shown expanded. Up and down arrows recall lines.

  komando database bigquery shell bq --write

commands.short: Run a query on a MySQL database (read only by default)
commands.long:
Run a query on a MySQL database (read only by default).

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first; when the query deletes data
(DROP, DELETE without WHERE, KILL, ...): dangerous, it cannot be undone: a
person types the name to go on, and an AI agent or a script needs
--allow-dangerous.

More about query:
A run stops after 30s unless --timeout (or the statement_timeout option in
the database URL) allows more. Placeholders take their values from
--arg, in order. -o csv and -o tsv print every row (up to --limit, if
given) for spreadsheets and scripts.
SQL that starts with a -- comment: pass it after -- or with -f -.

SQL Server has no read-only transaction: without --write komando rolls the
SQL back, and a statement it does not know as a read (a bare procedure
name, EXEC) needs --write. Its placeholders are @p1, @p2, ...

Oracle: placeholders are :1, :2, ... A PL/SQL block (BEGIN ... END;) runs
to the end of the text or to a line with only /, and needs --write and
--allow-dangerous. DDL (CREATE, ALTER, DROP, GRANT) commits on its own in
Oracle, so it needs --write, goes on its own, and a dry run only reports it.

ClickHouse has no transactions: without --write every request carries the
server's own readonly=1, and a statement that is not a read (INSERT, ALTER,
CREATE, ...) needs --write, goes on its own, and a dry run only reports it.
Placeholders are {p1:String}, {p2:UInt64}, ... (named p1, p2, with a type).

Snowflake has no read-only mode komando can switch on, and each statement
is a session of its own: without --write komando sends only what it rates
as a read, and a statement that is not a read needs --write, goes on its
own, and a dry run only reports it. Log in with a role that may only
read. Placeholders are ?.

BigQuery: each statement first goes as a dry run, which runs nothing and
says what BigQuery sees and how many bytes it would read (which is what
BigQuery bills). Without --write only a SELECT runs. A query that would
read more than --max-bytes (default 10GB) does not run, and the job
carries that cap too. A write needs --write, goes on its own, and
--write --dry-run shows BigQuery's dry run. Placeholders are ?; the values
go as STRING, so write CAST(? AS INT64) for a number.

On MongoDB the text is a command document in JSON, its first key
naming it ({"find": ...}, {"aggregate": ...}, {"update": ...}). komando rates
it as it rates SQL: what it does not know as a read needs --write. "$db"
picks another database than the URL's.
commands.example:
komando database mysql query shop-mysql "select id, email from users order by id desc limit 10"
  komando database mysql query shop-mysql --write --dry-run "update users set plan = 'pro' where id = 42"

commands.short: Load a backup into a MySQL database
commands.long:
Load a backup into a MySQL database.

Safety: dangerous, it cannot be undone: a person types the name to go on,
and an AI agent or a script needs --allow-dangerous.

More about restore:
Runs the SQL in FILE (from backup, pg_dump, mysqldump or any plain SQL
file; .gz is read compressed). komando runs the SQL itself, through the
conn's --via path, never with psql or mysql. A PostgreSQL archive (backup
--format custom) is recognized by its content and loaded with pg_restore
on a server: the one named with --run-on HOST, else the database's --via
server; the archive is streamed to it over SSH.

In a terminal komando first offers to save a copy of the database as it is
now (a backup), so you can go back. Scripts and AI agents get no question:
run backup yourself first.

A restore can overwrite existing data, so it needs --allow-dangerous, plus
--yes on a protected database. The whole file is checked first: client
commands that could run programs (\! or system) and SQL komando cannot
follow (a file ending inside a quote, a change to how quotes are read) are
refused, and SQL that runs programs, touches server files or changes
privileges is named in the approval.

PostgreSQL restores run in one transaction: on any error nothing changes.
MySQL runs the statements in order and stops at the first error.
commands.example:
komando database mysql restore shop-mysql --from shop-mysql.sql.gz --dry-run
  komando database mysql restore shop-mysql --from shop-mysql.sql.gz --allow-dangerous   # after a person's yes

statement ending in \G is shown expanded. Up and down arrows recall lines.

name, EXEC) needs --write. Its placeholders are @p1, @p2, ...

--allow-dangerous. DDL (CREATE, ALTER, DROP, GRANT) commits on its own in

server's own readonly=1, and a statement that is not a read (INSERT, ALTER,

as a read, and a statement that is not a read needs --write, goes on its

commands.short: Load a backup into a PostgreSQL database
commands.long:
Load a backup into a PostgreSQL database.

Safety: dangerous, it cannot be undone: a person types the name to go on,
and an AI agent or a script needs --allow-dangerous.

More about restore:
Runs the SQL in FILE (from backup, pg_dump, mysqldump or any plain SQL
file; .gz is read compressed). komando runs the SQL itself, through the
conn's --via path, never with psql or mysql. A PostgreSQL archive (backup
--format custom) is recognized by its content and loaded with pg_restore
on a server: the one named with --run-on HOST, else the database's --via
server; the archive is streamed to it over SSH.

now (a backup), so you can go back. Scripts and AI agents get no question:
run backup yourself first.

follow (a file ending inside a quote, a change to how quotes are read) are
refused, and SQL that runs programs, touches server files or changes
privileges is named in the approval.

MySQL runs the statements in order and stops at the first error.

streams the backup back over SSH. Without such a server (a direct
connection or a VPN) komando writes plain SQL itself. PostgreSQL can also
write its own archive with --format custom (compressed, restored with
pg_restore; needs pg_dump on a server). --table and --schema-only narrow
the backup. SQLite databases are copied as a database file instead. An
existing FILE is never overwritten. The file holds your data: it is
created readable only by you.

and tokens included, so an agent's backup needs a person, who runs it in
their own terminal.

commands.short: Run a query on a SQL Server database (read only by default)
commands.long:
Run a query on a SQL Server database (read only by default).

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first; when the query deletes data
(DROP, DELETE without WHERE, KILL, ...): dangerous, it cannot be undone: a
person types the name to go on, and an AI agent or a script needs
--allow-dangerous.

More about query:
A run stops after 30s unless --timeout (or the statement_timeout option in
the database URL) allows more. Placeholders take their values from
--arg, in order. -o csv and -o tsv print every row (up to --limit, if
given) for spreadsheets and scripts.
SQL that starts with a -- comment: pass it after -- or with -f -.

SQL Server has no read-only transaction: without --write komando rolls the
SQL back, and a statement it does not know as a read (a bare procedure
name, EXEC) needs --write. Its placeholders are @p1, @p2, ...

Oracle: placeholders are :1, :2, ... A PL/SQL block (BEGIN ... END;) runs
to the end of the text or to a line with only /, and needs --write and
--allow-dangerous. DDL (CREATE, ALTER, DROP, GRANT) commits on its own in
Oracle, so it needs --write, goes on its own, and a dry run only reports it.

ClickHouse has no transactions: without --write every request carries the
server's own readonly=1, and a statement that is not a read (INSERT, ALTER,
CREATE, ...) needs --write, goes on its own, and a dry run only reports it.
Placeholders are {p1:String}, {p2:UInt64}, ... (named p1, p2, with a type).

Snowflake has no read-only mode komando can switch on, and each statement
is a session of its own: without --write komando sends only what it rates
as a read, and a statement that is not a read needs --write, goes on its
own, and a dry run only reports it. Log in with a role that may only
read. Placeholders are ?.

BigQuery: each statement first goes as a dry run, which runs nothing and
says what BigQuery sees and how many bytes it would read (which is what
BigQuery bills). Without --write only a SELECT runs. A query that would
read more than --max-bytes (default 10GB) does not run, and the job
carries that cap too. A write needs --write, goes on its own, and
--write --dry-run shows BigQuery's dry run. Placeholders are ?; the values
go as STRING, so write CAST(? AS INT64) for a number.

On MongoDB the text is a command document in JSON, its first key
naming it ({"find": ...}, {"aggregate": ...}, {"update": ...}). komando rates
it as it rates SQL: what it does not know as a read needs --write. "$db"
picks another database than the URL's.
commands.example:
komando database sqlserver query sales-mssql "select top 10 id, email from users order by id desc"
  komando database sqlserver query sales-mssql --write --dry-run "update users set plan = 'pro' where id = 42"

flags.usage: the most rows to return per statement (0 = no limit; --max-output caps the size too)

commands.short: Open komando's SQL shell on a SQL Server database (person only)
commands.long:
Open komando's SQL shell on a SQL Server database.

Safety: only a person at a terminal can run it.

More about shell:
Opens komando's own SQL shell on the database, through its --via path when
it has one. Nothing else needs to be installed.

Each statement ends with ; (an Oracle PL/SQL block with a line holding
only /) and runs with the checks of query: read-only unless the shell was
started with --write, destructive statements only with --allow-dangerous,
and every statement is audited. A statement runs in its own transaction.
A protected conn asks first.

Inside: \q quits, \? lists the commands, \d [TABLE] shows tables or one
table, \l databases, \dn schemas, \du roles, \x switches expanded rows,
\timing shows how long each statement took, \i FILE runs a file, and a
statement ending in \G is shown expanded. Up and down arrows recall lines.
commands.example:

  komando database sqlserver shell sales-mssql --write
  komando database sqlserver shell sales-mssql --write --dry-run

  komando db grant prod-db app_ro --privileges SELECT --on all-tables:public --allow-dangerous   # after a person's yes
  komando db grant prod-db app_ro --role readers --dry-run
  komando db grant prod-db app_ro --role readers --allow-dangerous   # after a person's yes
  komando db grant prod-db app --privileges SELECT,INSERT,UPDATE --on 'shop.*' --dry-run

commands.short: Stop a session's running query (--session ends the connection)
commands.long:
Find the PID with `komando db activity` or `komando db locks`. Without
--session only the running query stops (its transaction rolls back) and the
client stays connected. --dry-run shows the session it would stop. SQL
Server can only end a session (KILL), so there it needs --session. On Oracle
the PID is the SID that db activity shows. On ClickHouse it is the number db
activity shows for the query (made from its query_id); ClickHouse stops
queries, not connections, so there is no --session. On Snowflake, too, the
PID is the number db activity shows for the query; --session ends its
session (SYSTEM$ABORT_SESSION). On BigQuery it is the number db activity
shows for a job, which db kill cancels (jobs.cancel); there is no --session.
On MongoDB the PID is the opid that db activity shows; db kill stops that
operation (killOp) and the client stays connected, so there is no --session.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first; on a protected server or
conn, a person's yes (--yes) as well.
commands.example:
komando db kill prod-db 4821 --dry-run
  komando db kill prod-db 4821
  komando db kill prod-db 4821 --session --dry-run
  komando db kill prod-db 4821 --session --allow-dangerous   # after a person's yes

commands.short: Run a command in a container (its words are passed as given, no shell)
commands.long:
Runs COMMAND in the container with its arguments exactly as written (like
`docker exec`): no shell is added, so the image needs no sh. For pipes or
&& write the shell yourself: -- sh -c 'a | b'. The destructive-command
policy checks the command; --read-only declares that it only looks: only
commands komando knows only read run, and a protected server then needs
no --yes.

destructive rule: dangerous, it cannot be undone: a person types the name to
go on, and an AI agent or a script needs --allow-dangerous; on a protected
server or conn, a person's yes (--yes) as well.
commands.example:
komando docker exec app1 api -- php artisan migrate:status
  komando docker exec app1 api --read-only -- sh -c 'ls /data | wc -l'

commands.short: Free disk space: stopped containers, unused images, build cache
commands.long:
Runs docker system prune on the server. It removes stopped containers,
dangling images (--all: every image no container uses), unused networks
and build cache; with --volumes also unused anonymous volumes and the data
in them.
--older-than 30d keeps everything made in the last 30 days. Docker has no
age filter for volumes, so with --volumes komando reads each unused
anonymous volume's creation time and removes only the older ones
(docker volume rm NAME), after the prune.

Safety: dangerous, it cannot be undone: a person types the name to go on,
and an AI agent or a script needs --allow-dangerous; on a protected server
or conn, a person's yes (--yes) as well.

--dry-run changes nothing: it lists what would go, with sizes and a total,
read from docker on the server. The real run deletes and needs
--allow-dangerous; a protected server needs --yes too.
commands.example:
komando docker prune web1 --dry-run
  komando docker prune web1 --older-than 30d --all --dry-run
  komando docker prune web1 --older-than 30d --dry-run
  komando docker prune web1 --older-than 30d --allow-dangerous   # after a person's yes
  komando docker prune web1 --volumes --older-than 30d --dry-run

commands.short: The environment variables komando reads
commands.long:
The environment variables komando reads.

  KOMANDO_HOME        where komando keeps its data (default ~/.komando)
  KOMANDO_OUTPUT      json or text when -o is not given
  KOMANDO_ACTOR       the name the audit log gives you
  KOMANDO_AGENT=1     an AI agent komando does not know by itself
  KOMANDO_VAULT_PASS  the vault passphrase, when the vault has one
  CI                  a CI job: komando never asks anything
  NO_COLOR            no colors

commands.short: What komando's exit codes mean
commands.long:
What komando's exit codes mean.

  0 ok          1 error           2 usage           3 not found
  4 connect     5 failed on the server              6 blocked for safety
  7 timeout     8 precondition or conflict

-o json shows the error code (USAGE, PROTECTED_TARGET ...) and a hint.

commands.short: Save servers, conns, VPNs, recipes and settings to a file
commands.long:
Saves your list to a file (komando-export/1, always JSON) that
`komando import komando FILE` reads on another computer. Passwords and key
files are never in it (only in a sealed file); it lists the secrets and keys
to bring along. With a
TARGET (@prod, kind:host, web1,web2) only those servers, conns and VPNs are
saved; without one also your recipes, deny rules and settings. Without --to
it prints the same JSON.

Safety: it only reads; with --sealed: only a person at a terminal can run
it; with --for-phone: only a person at a terminal can run it; on a protected
server or conn, a person's yes (--yes) as well.

--sealed writes the same list with the passwords it uses into one sealed
file, for moving to another computer: komando asks for a passphrase twice
(15 or more characters), hidden, and the file opens only with it.
--for-phone seals the file to the iPhone app's key instead: komando asks
for the key file the phone shared and the key check the phone shows. Both
print a check phrase of six words; the phone shows the same words for the
file it got. --with-keys adds the private keys the servers use.

Only a person at a terminal can make a sealed file: an AI agent gets
NEEDS_PERSON, and a dry run says what would be sealed.
commands.example:
komando export --to komando-backup.json
  komando export @prod --to prod.json
  komando export kind:host --to servers.json
  komando import komando komando-backup.json      # on the other computer
  komando export --sealed --to move.kmdseal       # with passwords; asks a passphrase
  komando export --for-phone --to phone.kmdseal   # for the iPhone app; asks for its key

commands.short: Files on servers: read, edit, undo an edit, move, remove
commands.long:
Reads and changes files on servers over SFTP and returns structured results.
Use --sudo for files that root owns: a read runs `sudo cat`, a write goes to
a temporary file first and then into place with `sudo install`.

For an agent, `fs replace` is the way to edit a config file: it fails unless
the old text matches exactly once (or --all), and --backup keeps a .bak
copy.
commands.example:
komando fs list web1 /etc/nginx
  komando fs cat web1 /etc/nginx/nginx.conf
  komando fs replace web1 /etc/nginx/nginx.conf --old 'worker_connections 512' --new 'worker_connections 1024' --backup --dry-run
  komando fs replace web1 /etc/nginx/nginx.conf --old 'worker_connections 512' --new 'worker_connections 1024' --backup
  komando fs restore web1 /etc/nginx/nginx.conf     # undo the edit

commands.usage: komando fs replace TARGET PATH --old TEXT --new TEXT [flags]
commands.short: Edit a file on servers by replacing exact text
commands.long:
Replaces --old with --new in PATH. On a group (@web) every server gets the
same edit; each server's result says what changed there, and a server where
--old is not found fails on its own (NO_MATCH) while the others are changed.
Run it with --dry-run first to see each server's diff.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first; on a protected server or
conn, a person's yes (--yes) as well.

komando fs replace web1 /etc/nginx/nginx.conf --old 'worker_connections 768;' --new 'worker_connections 4096;' --sudo --backup
  komando fs replace @web /etc/nginx/nginx.conf --old 'worker_connections 768;' --new 'worker_connections 4096;' --sudo --backup --dry-run
  komando fs replace web1 /etc/ssh/sshd_config --regex --old '(?m)^#?PasswordAuthentication .*$' --new 'PasswordAuthentication no' --sudo

Puts back the newest backup of PATH that fs write or fs replace --backup

it is now is kept as a new backup first, so you can undo the restore too.
On a group (@web) each server puts back its own newest backup. Add --dry-run
to see the change without making it.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first; on a protected server or
conn, a person's yes (--yes) as well.

  komando fs restore web1 /etc/nginx/nginx.conf --copy /etc/nginx/nginx.conf.bak --sudo

and an AI agent or a script needs --allow-dangerous; on a protected server
or conn, a person's yes (--yes) as well.

komando fs rm web1 /tmp/upload.tar.gz

  komando fs rm web1 /srv/app/releases/old --recursive --allow-dangerous   # after a person's yes

commands.short: Bring in what you have: ssh config, .pgpass, my.cnf, .env
commands.long:
Adds servers, conns, VPNs and recipes from files you already have.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first; SOURCE kubeconfig, when an AI
agent imports a context whose login runs a program or sends a file of this
computer: it weakens a safety check: a person's yes (--yes); SOURCE komando,
when the file is sealed (export --sealed): a person types its passphrase:
only a person at a terminal can run it; when an imported proxy command
matches a destructive rule: dangerous, it cannot be undone: a person types
the name to go on, and an AI agent or a script needs --allow-dangerous; when
an AI agent imports a server with a proxy command: it weakens a safety
check: a person's yes (--yes).

Sources:
  ssh-config  servers from your OpenSSH config (default ~/.ssh/config)
  pgpass      PostgreSQL databases and their passwords (default ~/.pgpass)
  mycnf       MySQL/MariaDB databases from [client] sections (default ~/.my.cnf)
  env         database, cache and storage URLs (DATABASE_URL, REDIS_URL, ...) (default .env)
  kubeconfig  Kubernetes clusters, one conn per context (default ~/.kube/config)
  docker      container registries you are logged in to (default ~/.docker/config.json)
  filezilla   SFTP sites from FileZilla's Site Manager (default ~/.config/filezilla/sitemanager.xml)
  rclone      SFTP remotes from rclone (default ~/.config/rclone/rclone.conf)
  putty       SSH sessions from PuTTY (a .reg file: `reg export HKCU\Software\SimonTatham\PuTTY\Sessions putty.reg`)
  mobaxterm   SSH sessions from MobaXterm (a .mxtsessions file: right-click User sessions, Export all sessions to file)
  securecrt   SSH2 sessions from SecureCRT (File > Export Settings gives an .xml file; or its Sessions folder)
  aws         an S3 storage conn per bucket of each AWS profile (uses the profile; no key is copied) (default ~/.aws/config)
  aws-ec2     a server per running EC2 instance of each AWS profile, in its region (read only, with the profile's login) (default ~/.aws/config)
  dbeaver     databases from DBeaver (passwords set afterwards) (default ~/Library/DBeaverData/workspace6/General/.dbeaver/data-sources.json)
  komando     a file made by `komando export` (moving to another computer)
  csv         servers from a spreadsheet (CSV, first row names the columns: name, address (or ip), user, port, key, identity, password-ref, sudo-ref, via, groups (or role), tags, protected, notes)

Passwords go to the vault (as <name>-pass; a kubeconfig as
<name>-kubeconfig) and are referenced from the conn; they are never
printed. Existing names are skipped unless
--overwrite (replacing a protected one also needs --yes). Proxy commands
from an ssh config run on this computer, so an AI agent needs a person's yes
for them. Try --dry-run first to see what would be added.
commands.example:
komando import ssh-config --dry-run
  komando import pgpass
  komando import env ./app/.env --group shop
  komando import komando backup.json

commands.short: Log in to AWS IAM Identity Center for a profile (person only)
commands.long:
Opens the AWS sign-in page in your browser and waits until you confirm the
code shown here. The login is saved where the aws CLI keeps it
(~/.aws/sso/cache), so komando, the AWS SDKs and the aws CLI all use it. The
profile is the one in ~/.aws/config with sso_start_url or sso_session, or a
profile that assumes a role from one (source_profile).

Safety: only a person at a terminal can run it.

Conns that name the profile (--option aws_profile=NAME) use the login until
it runs out; then their commands stop with AWS_LOGIN_REQUIRED and the same
command renews it. Logging in is for a person: an AI agent gets
NEEDS_PERSON and asks you to run it. A profile with keys in
~/.aws/credentials needs no login.

komando login aws --profile prod       # opens the browser; confirm the code shown
  komando login aws                      # the profile in AWS_PROFILE, else default
  komando login aws --profile prod --dry-run   # which sign-in page, without logging in

apt-get --only-upgrade of the listed packages, keeping changed config
files. On dnf/yum it runs "upgrade --security", on zypper "patch
--category security". needrestart is kept from
restarting services during the run; the result lists the services that
need it.

After each server komando compares the state with the one before. When fewer
containers run or a unit has failed, it stops and leaves the other servers
as they are (--keep-going patches them anyway). It never reboots:
reboot_required says when a server needs one, use `komando host ssh exec
TARGET --sudo --allow-dangerous -- reboot`.

The upgrade runs detached on the server, so a dropped connection does not
break it. It waits up to 30 minutes per server (--timeout changes it).
Where komando cannot pick the security updates (apk, pacman, dnf/yum
repositories without security notices) the server stops with
SECURITY_UNSUPPORTED: use `komando pkg upgrade` without --security there.
commands.example:
komando pkg upgrade web1 --dry-run   # see what would change first
  komando pkg upgrade web1 openssl
  komando pkg upgrade @web --security --dry-run
  komando pkg upgrade @web --security

commands.short: Switch a rule off or on, everywhere or on some servers
commands.long:
--off switches a rule off, so it no longer stops a command. With
--add-server or --add-group it is off only on those servers (a group as its
servers are now): a command that also runs on another server is still
stopped. Switching a rule off weakens a safety check, so komando asks first:
an AI agent's request opens the approval window on your screen, and for a
rule that keeps the others working (check-failed, decode-run, rm-root, mkfs,
sshd-stop, ...) you type the rule's name at a terminal, with --yes too, and
an AI agent's request for one is refused. The audit log keeps every switch,
and `komando doctor` names every rule that is off. --off=false switches it
on again everywhere; --rm-server and --rm-group switch it on again on those
servers only.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first; unless it only switches the
rule on: it weakens a safety check: a person's yes (--yes).
commands.example:
komando policy edit docker-prune --off --add-server build1
  komando policy edit docker-prune --off --add-server build1 --dry-run
  komando policy edit pkg-remove-essential --off --add-group lab
  komando policy edit docker-prune --rm-server build1
  komando policy edit docker-prune --off=false

Read and send messages on Kafka, RabbitMQ, NATS, SQS and Pub/Sub. Add a
queue with `komando queue kafka add` (or rabbitmq, nats, sqs, pubsub).

gives RabbitMQ and Pub/Sub messages straight back, reads NATS stream
messages by their number, and receives SQS messages without hiding or
deleting them, so nothing is removed. message create and topic create
change (production queues ask first); topic delete and message delete
--all delete messages, so they also need --allow-dangerous. Try any change
with --dry-run first. In RabbitMQ words a topic is a queue; in NATS words
it is a stream. Pub/Sub keeps messages in subscriptions: message list and
message delete --all take a subscription, and consumer list lists them.

Look at, copy and clean up container images. Add a registry with
`komando registry oci add ghcr registry://myuser@ghcr.io --ask-password`,
or bring in the ones you use with `komando import docker`.
ls and inspect only read, copy writes to the destination, rm and prune
delete images and need --allow-dangerous (try --dry-run first).

TLS options in the registry URL: ?ca=credential:NAME trusts a private CA (or
pins the registry's own certificate; the check stays on), ?tls=skip-verify
does not check the certificate, ?tls=false is plain HTTP. ?resolve=IP
connects to that IP instead of what DNS says (like curl --resolve). With
--via the last server looks the name up.
commands.example:
komando registry oci add ghcr registry://myuser@ghcr.io --ask-password
  komando registry oci image list ghcr myorg/api
  komando registry oci image show ghcr myorg/api:1.4.2
  komando registry oci image copy ghcr:myorg/api:1.4.2 harbor:prod/api:1.4.2
  komando registry oci image prune harbor prod/api --keep 10 --dry-run

commands.short: Rename one entry, or all names starting with OLD (--starts-with)
commands.long:
Without --starts-with: renames the one server, conn, VPN, secret, key or
group named OLD, as `komando host ssh rename` and the others do. When OLD
names two kinds of entry (a server and a secret), it says which commands to
use.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first.

With --starts-with: renames every server, conn, VPN, secret, key and group
whose name starts with OLD: OLD is replaced with NEW. When OLD ends in -,
the name OLD without it is renamed too (--starts-with shop- acme-shop- turns
group shop into acme-shop).

Every reference follows, as with `host rename` and `credential password
rename`: --via paths, password, sudo, key, preshared key and passphrase
references, credential:NAME options in conn URLs, the key a server uses,
group membership, exec sessions and tunnels. A key komando made (credential
key create) lives in the sealed store, so no file moves; a key file you
added stays where it is. The protected mark, labels, notes and creation time
stay. Names inside URLs (a bucket, a database user) are the resource's own
and do not change.

--in-notes also replaces old names in notes, and --in-labels in label
values: server, conn, VPN and secret names as whole words, a group written
@NAME, and a pattern such as shop-db-* when it matches the same entries
after the rename. OLD without its -, group names without @, key names, and a
name that is also the user, host, bucket or database in a conn URL stay:
they often mean something else. The result lists each one it keeps ("kept"),
and each label value that names an old entry, with or without --in-labels.

Everything changes in one step, or nothing does: a new name that is taken
(or two old names that would get one new name) stops it before anything
is written. When NEW starts with OLD, names that start with NEW already
are left alone, so a second run changes nothing.

Renaming protected servers and conns needs --yes once, for all of them
(an AI agent's --yes opens one window for a person). See what would change
with --dry-run first. --kind renames only some kinds; references still
follow.
To rename one entry, use host ssh rename, conn rename, vpn rename,
credential password rename, credential key rename or group rename.
commands.example:
komando rename web1 web-01 --dry-run                 # one entry, whatever kind it is
  komando rename --starts-with shop- acme-shop- --dry-run   # the old -> new list and every reference
  komando rename --starts-with shop- acme-shop- --yes   # after a person's yes
  komando rename --starts-with old-registry registry --kind conn,secret
  komando rename --starts-with lab- test- --in-notes --in-labels --dry-run

flags.name: in-labels
flags.usage: also replace old names in label values, as --in-notes does (label names stay)

flags.name: in-notes
flags.usage: also replace old names in notes (server, conn, VPN and secret names, @group, OLD* patterns)

flags.name: kind
flags.usage: rename only these kinds: host, conn, vpn, secret, key, group (default: all)

flags.name: starts-with
flags.usage: rename every name that starts with OLD

commands.short: How komando keeps a change from going wrong
commands.long:
How komando keeps a change from going wrong.

  --dry-run           every change can show what it would do first
  protected targets   a change asks [y/N] at your terminal; scripts and agents need --yes
  dangerous commands  rm -rf /, DROP DATABASE ...: you type the name; scripts need --allow-dangerous
  read only           database KIND query, cache redis raw and cluster kubernetes raw only read unless you add --write
  audit               komando audit list shows every change and who asked for it

An AI agent is never asked: it gets exit 6 and a person allows the flag in a
window on the screen. See docs/features/safety.md.

commands.short: Every command, flag and exit code, machine-readable
commands.long: Machine-readable reference of every command, flag, exit code and selector.
commands.example:
komando schema            # everything
  komando schema exec        # one command subtree
  komando schema host.add    # one command, as named in the envelope
  komando schema --compact   # paths + short descriptions only

flags.name: compact
flags.usage: only paths and short descriptions

commands.short: Check or copy a saved password or token
commands.long:
Save a password once, then point to it as credential:NAME instead of typing
it:
  komando credential password add web1-pass
  komando host ssh edit web1 --credential web1-pass

komando shows a saved value only to a person: at a terminal with `credential
password show --reveal`, or after "Allow once" in komando's window; never to
an AI agent. `secret check` compares a value with the saved one without
showing either. `credential password rename` and `secret cp` rename and
copy.

How it is stored: each secret sealed with AES-256-GCM in
~/.komando/store.db. The random key is in the OS keychain (or in store.key
where there is none, or with KOMANDO_KEYCHAIN=off), or comes from
$KOMANDO_VAULT_PASS when that is set at first use (`config vault passphrase`
changes it).

A --password-ref (and the other -ref flags) can also read a password your
team keeps elsewhere; komando reads it when needed and never stores it:
  env:VAR  file:PATH  vault:PATH#FIELD  aws-sm:NAME[#KEY]  gcp-sm:NAME[@PROJECT]
  azure-kv:VAULT/NAME[#KEY]  op://VAULT/ITEM/FIELD  bw://ITEM/FIELD  kdbx:FILE#GROUP/ENTRY
commands.example:
komando secret check db-pass   # type the value to compare, hidden
  komando secret cp db-pass db-pass-old --dry-run
  komando secret cp db-pass db-pass-old

commands.short: Compare a typed value to a secret without showing either (person only)
commands.long:
Asks for a value (hidden, or from --from-env VAR or a pipe) and says whether
it is the stored one. When it is not, it says how they differ (only spaces
at the ends, only upper and lower case, or the number of characters), but
never shows either value.

Safety: only a person at a terminal can run it.

Only a person can run it: for an AI agent, a yes/no answer about a value it
picks would be a way to guess the secret one try at a time.
commands.example:
komando secret check vpn-pass            # type or paste it after the prompt
  pbpaste | komando secret check vpn-pass

flags.name: from-env
flags.usage: read the value to compare from this environment variable

commands.short: Copy a secret to a new name in the vault (value never shown)
commands.long:
Stores the value of OLD under NEW as well. The value stays inside the vault:
it is never printed, so an AI agent can do this too. Nothing that uses OLD
changes.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first.

When NEW exists already, --overwrite replaces its value; when a protected
server or conn uses NEW, that also needs --yes.
commands.example:
komando secret cp db-pass db-pass-old
  komando secret cp db-pass db-pass-old --dry-run
  komando secret cp web-pass shared-pass --overwrite

commands.short: Let an SSH key run komando here and nothing else (person only)
commands.long:
ssh-gate lets an SSH key (a phone's, say) run komando on this computer, and
nothing else: no shell, no file copy, no port forwarding. Add the key to
~/.ssh/authorized_keys with the line `komando ssh-gate line` prints; sshd
then runs ssh-gate for it, whatever the key asks for.

Safety: only a person at a terminal can run it.

ssh-gate takes the command the key sent (SSH_ORIGINAL_COMMAND) only when it
is one komando command. It splits it into words like a shell, but expands
nothing and runs no shell: ; | & > < $ and backquotes are refused unless
they are quoted. One KOMANDO_AGENT=NAME may come before komando.

komando then runs as for an AI agent: secret values stay [hidden], --reveal
and --allow-dangerous are refused, and --yes for a protected server needs a
person on this computer. Commands that need a person at a terminal (shell,
database KIND shell, config vault passphrase ...) are refused (a
--shell-access key may open `komando host ssh shell SERVER`: see ssh-gate
line; that shell is full control of the server, outside these rules). The
key runs commands on servers, never one that writes on this computer or
reads a file here (a script, SQL or upload source by path; '-' for the key's
own input works): no copy to a file here (copy SRC - streams to the key's
own output), no change to servers, VPNs, settings, rules, secrets, keys or
recipes in komando, no update, no change on a sqlite file or a target at
localhost or 127.x. With --read-only only commands that read run (database
KIND query and cache redis raw without --write), and only those that stay on
the servers and conns in your list: no net, no cert check of a website, no
exec, docker exec, cluster kubernetes exec or snippet exec, unless the line
also has --network. `komando ssh-gate status` tells a key which it is. Every
command a key runs or is refused is in `komando audit list`, with --name,
even when the audit setting is off.
commands.example:
komando ssh-gate line --name phone ~/phone.pub
  komando ssh-gate line --name phone-read --read-only 'ssh-ed25519 AAAA... phone'
commands.kind_note: runs the komando command an SSH key sent, when ssh-gate allows it

commands.short: Print the authorized_keys line that limits a key to komando
commands.long:
Prints the line to add to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on this computer, so the
key runs komando through ssh-gate and nothing else. PUBLIC_KEY is the key's
line (ssh-ed25519 AAAA... comment) or a .pub file holding it. The line names
this komando by its full path, as sshd does not search PATH.

A --read-only key runs only commands that read, and only those that stay on
the servers and conns in your list: no net checks, no cert check of a
website, and no exec, docker exec, cluster kubernetes exec or snippet exec,
whose programs can connect anywhere and carry what they read in a URL or a
DNS name. Add --network too for a read key that may do those.

With --shell-access (not with --read-only) the key may also open a login
shell on one server: ssh -t HOST komando host ssh shell SERVER, word for
word. Its line has restrict,pty, so sshd gives it a terminal when it asks
for one. The shell is refused on a protected server, a Windows server or
this computer, with any other word or flag, without the terminal, and on
every server while you have deny rules of your own (komando policy list); db
shell and cluster kubernetes shell stay refused. On the servers it opens on,
the shell is full control of the server, as the account komando logs in
with: what is typed is outside komando's per-command rules, masking and
audit. Give such a key only to a device you would give that login to. Each
session's start and end are in komando audit list (key, server, how long,
why it ended), and a session with no input and no output for 30 minutes
ends.
commands.example:
komando ssh-gate line --name phone ~/phone.pub
  komando ssh-gate line --name phone-read --read-only 'ssh-ed25519 AAAA... phone'
  komando ssh-gate line --name phone-checks --read-only --network ~/phone.pub
  komando ssh-gate line --name ops --shell-access ~/ops.pub

flags.name: name
flags.usage: the key's name in the audit log (required)

flags.name: network
flags.usage: with --read-only: the key may also run reads that reach the network (net, cert check of a URL, exec --read-only)

flags.name: read-only
flags.usage: the key runs only commands that read

flags.name: shell-access
flags.usage: the key may also open a login shell on one server (ssh -t HOST komando host ssh shell SERVER); not with --read-only

commands.short: Say which ssh-gate key runs this, and what it may do
commands.long:
Through an SSH key that ssh-gate limits, prints the key's name and what it
may do: change things, or read only, whether its reads may reach the network
(--network on its line), and whether it may open a login shell on a server
(--shell-access on its line), and whether it acts on this server only (here:
a phone's key on a server, see credential key install --public-key-file).
ssh-gate answers it itself, so an app can check what its key is before it
sends anything else. Typed on the komando computer, it says the command did
not come through a key.
commands.example:
ssh HOST komando ssh-gate status -o json
  komando ssh-gate status

commands.short: What komando left running: VPNs, logins, tunnels, exec sessions
commands.long:
Lists what still runs after the command that started it ended: VPN sessions
(from vpn KIND start, or started by a command), server logins kept by
`komando login SERVER`, AWS IAM Identity Center (SSO) logins of the profiles
in ~/.aws/config and when they end, tunnels, and the exec sessions started
on servers. Nothing is contacted, so it is quick and works offline. An exec
session is listed until `komando host ssh exec TARGET --attach ID --remove`
(or a read to its end by the one who started it) removes it; whether it
still runs is known on its server: `komando host ssh exec TARGET --attach
ID` reads it.

--short prints one line for your shell prompt: "vpn:1 tun:2" when one VPN
is up and two tunnels run, nothing when nothing runs. It reads only the
process numbers komando keeps beside its sealed store (no names, no key),
prints no JSON and never fails, so it is safe to run on every prompt.

zsh (also with oh-my-zsh), in ~/.zshrc:
  setopt PROMPT_SUBST
  RPROMPT='$(komando status --short)'

bash, in ~/.bashrc:
  PS1='$(p=$(komando status --short); [ -n "$p" ] && echo "[$p] ")'"$PS1"

starship, in ~/.config/starship.toml:
  [custom.komando]
  command = "komando status --short"
  when = true
commands.example:
komando status
  komando status -o json
  komando status --short   # prints for example vpn:2 tun:1, or nothing
