commands.short: Check that servers, conns and VPNs answer and let you in
commands.long:
Logs in to each server (and checks who it is and whether sudo needs a
password), connects to each conn and checks each VPN.

--wait 5m waits for new servers: komando tests again every few seconds until
every target passes or the time is up, for example right after a cloud
server was created or rebuilt. It does not wait out a changed host key
(HOSTKEY_MISMATCH), a refused login (AUTH_FAILED: retrying could get your
address banned), a VPN that needs a login, or a local key or secret problem:
those fail at once. To wait for the server's own start-up too, run `komando
host ssh exec TARGET --read-only -- cloud-init status --wait` next.

A server that asks for a password or a two-factor code only a person can
answer: when a person runs test at a terminal, komando asks once and keeps
the session open for the login_for setting (8 hours). An AI agent's commands
to that server reuse the session; when it has expired they fail and name
this command, and an agent never types a code. --end closes the kept session
of the servers it names, or of every server when it names none; `komando
status` lists the kept sessions.
commands.example:
komando test @prod
  komando test all
  komando test @new --wait 5m   # right after creating servers
  komando test --end            # end every kept session

flags.name: end
flags.usage: end the kept sessions of the servers named (every server when none is named), instead of testing

flags.name: wait
flags.usage: test again every few seconds until every target passes, for up to this long (like 5m)

commands.short: Update komando to the newest release
commands.long:
Replaces this komando program with the newest release from GitHub, or with
the VERSION you name. It checks that the release is signed with the komando
project's key (a release without that signature is refused), checks the
download against the release's signed checksums.txt, and tries the new
program before it replaces the old one. If anything fails, the old komando
stays as it was.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first; when it installs an older
version: it weakens a safety check: a person's yes (--yes).

See whether there is a newer version, changing nothing: komando update
--dry-run.

komando lives in a folder only root may change (/usr/local/bin, for
example)? Then run it with sudo: sudo komando update. As root it writes
nothing in ~/.komando; otherwise the update goes into the audit log like
other changes.

Going back to an older version needs a person's yes (--yes for an agent): an
older komando may lack safety checks this one has. Without a VERSION it
never goes back.

A komando built from source that is not a release (make build, or go build
of a commit between releases) is not replaced: build it again instead. One
that reports a release version (go install ...@v0.12.0, or go build at a
release tag) counts as that release and is replaced. --timeout limits the
whole update (default 10m).
commands.example:
komando update --dry-run    # is there a newer version?
  komando update              # install the newest release
  sudo komando update         # komando is in /usr/local/bin
  komando update v0.14.0      # install this version

confirm.when: when it installs an older version

commands.short: Print the komando version and its home folder

commands.short: VPNs komando connects when a path needs one: add, connect, check
commands.long:
Add a VPN once, then put it first in --via. A command that needs it
connects it, using the login you saved. The word after vpn is the kind:

  komando vpn wireguard add office --config ~/Downloads/office.conf
  komando vpn globalprotect add client-x --portal vpn.client.com --user alice --credential client-x --mfa
  komando host ssh add app admin@10.0.0.5 --via office,bastion
  komando host ssh exec app -- uptime

VPNs with --mfa need a person: run `komando vpn KIND start NAME` once and
later commands (and agents) reuse that session. komando never answers MFA.

Kinds:
  anyconnect    Cisco AnyConnect / ocserv, run inside komando (no openconnect)
  f5            F5 BIG-IP SSL VPN
  fortinet      Fortinet SSL VPN (FortiClient)
  globalprotect Palo Alto GlobalProtect
  ikev2         IKEv2/IPsec (pre-shared key or EAP login with a server certificate), run inside komando
  ipsec         Cisco-style IPsec (IKEv1, group name and XAUTH login), run inside komando
  l2tp          L2TP/IPsec with a pre-shared key, run inside komando (no admin rights)
  openvpn       OpenVPN, also Pritunl profiles, run inside komando (no openvpn program, Docker or admin rights)
  proxy         an HTTP proxy (CONNECT), such as a company proxy: every connection is tunneled through it
  pulse         Pulse Secure / Ivanti Connect Secure
  socks         a SOCKS5 proxy that is already running (`komando host ssh tunnel start TARGET -D`, a company proxy)
  system        a VPN set up in your computer's settings; --service lets `vpn KIND start` connect it
  tailscale     Tailscale or Headscale, run inside komando (no tailscaled, no admin rights)
  wireguard     WireGuard, run inside komando (no admin rights, many at once)
commands.example:
komando vpn wireguard add office --config ~/Downloads/office.conf
  komando vpn wireguard test office
  komando host ssh edit db1 --via office --dry-run
  komando vpn wireguard start office

commands.short: Change saved WireGuard VPNs (only the flags you give)
commands.long:
Change saved WireGuard VPNs (only the flags you give).

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first; with --mfa=false: it weakens
a safety check: a person's yes (--yes); with --protected=false or --unset
protected: it weakens a safety check: a person's yes (--yes); on a protected
server or conn, a person's yes (--yes) as well.
commands.example:
komando vpn wireguard edit office --check 10.0.0.5:22
  komando vpn wireguard edit @office --protected --dry-run

env.KOMANDO_ACTOR: name recorded in the audit log (for example claude-agent)
env.KOMANDO_KEYCHAIN: off: komando uses no keychain, and a new vault keeps its key in store.key (CI, containers)
env.KOMANDO_VAULT_PASS: vault passphrase (optional; otherwise the key is in the OS keychain, or store.key where there is none; komando config vault passphrase sets or changes it)

envelope.data: command-specific result; multi-host commands use data.results[] + data.summary
envelope.error: {code, message, hint} when ok=false (data may still be present for partial failures)
envelope.meta: {contract, version, duration_ms, dry_run}, and when they apply: would_be_blocked (a dry run's stop), skipped (targets a command cannot use), host_keys_pinned, truncated (a list stopped at --limit; --limit 0 shows all)

exit_codes.4: connection/auth/host-key failure, or the connection broke mid-command (CONNECTION_LOST: outcome unknown)
exit_codes.6: blocked for safety: needs a person's yes (the flag error.hint names) or a person at a terminal
exit_codes.8: precondition failed (for example replace text not found / ambiguous)

global_flags.name: allow-dangerous
global_flags.usage: run a command the safety rules would block

global_flags.name: connect-timeout
global_flags.usage: time to connect, like 30s (default: setting connect_timeout, 15s)

global_flags.name: dry-run
global_flags.usage: show what would run, changing nothing

global_flags.name: host-key-policy
global_flags.usage: accept-new, strict or off: how a server's key is checked (default: setting host_key_policy, accept-new)

global_flags.name: max-output
global_flags.usage: bytes kept per stream per server, like 1MiB (default: setting max_output_bytes, 256KiB)

global_flags.name: output
global_flags.usage:
json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
text in a terminal, JSON when piped); database KIND
query also takes csv and tsv

global_flags.name: reveal
global_flags.usage: show passwords and keys in output (an agent needs a person's yes)

global_flags.name: timeout
global_flags.usage: time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)

global_flags.name: yes
global_flags.usage: confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)

data.name: komando
data.secret_refs: credential:NAME (komando's vault) | env:VAR | file:PATH | op://VAULT/ITEM/FIELD (1Password Connect) | bw://ITEM/FIELD (Bitwarden, Vaultwarden) | kdbx:FILE#GROUP/ENTRY[#FIELD] (KeePass, KeePassXC) | vault:PATH#FIELD (HashiCorp Vault or OpenBao, KV) | aws-sm:NAME[#JSON_KEY] (AWS Secrets Manager) | gcp-sm:NAME[@PROJECT] (Google Secret Manager) | azure-kv:VAULT/NAME[#JSON_KEY] (Azure Key Vault)
data.selector_note: a selector picks servers and conns together; each command uses the ones it works with and lists the rest in meta.skipped

target_selectors.@GROUP: everything in a group (servers and conns)
target_selectors.NAME: a server, conn or VPN from your list
target_selectors.kind:KIND: by type: host, conn, vpn, a conn kind (postgres, redis, s3, ...), a command family (db, cache, queue, storage, cluster, registry) or a VPN kind
target_selectors.label:KEY=VAL: everything with a label (label:KEY = any value)
target_selectors.os:OS: servers by system: os:windows or os:linux
target_selectors.user@addr:port: ad-hoc server not in your list
